---
title: "Getting Started"
---

This guide will help you get up and running with DeckGL.jl.

## Installation

DeckGL.jl can be installed from GitHub:

```julia
using Pkg
Pkg.add(url="https://github.com/RallypointOne/DeckGL.jl")
```

## Basic Concepts

DeckGL.jl has three main components:

1. **Layers** - Define what data to visualize and how
2. **ViewState** - Configure the camera (position, zoom, angle)
3. **Deck** - Container that combines layers, view state, and the basemap

## Your First Visualization

Let's create a simple scatterplot over a basemap:

```{julia}
using DeckGL

# Sample data - any Tables.jl-compatible source works
data = (
    lng = [-122.4, -122.5, -122.3, -122.45, -122.35],
    lat = [37.8, 37.7, 37.9, 37.75, 37.85],
    size = [100, 200, 150, 180, 120]
)

# Create a layer
layer = ScatterplotLayer(
    data = data,
    get_position = [:lng, :lat],         # Reference columns by symbol
    get_radius = :size,                  # Data-driven radius
    get_fill_color = [255, 140, 0, 200], # RGBA color
    radius_min_pixels = 4
)

# Create the deck
deck = Deck(
    layer,
    initial_view_state = ViewState(
        longitude = -122.4,
        latitude = 37.8,
        zoom = 11
    ),
    map_style = "https://basemaps.cartocdn.com/gl/positron-gl-style/style.json"
)
```

In a notebook or on this page a `Deck` displays itself. Elsewhere, `open_html(deck)`
opens it in a browser and `save_html(deck, "map.html")` writes it to a file.

## Basemaps

`map_style` is the URL of a [MapLibre](https://maplibre.org/) style, drawn underneath the
layers. Carto publishes several that are free and need no API key:

| Style | URL |
|-------|-----|
| Positron (light) | `https://basemaps.cartocdn.com/gl/positron-gl-style/style.json` |
| Dark Matter | `https://basemaps.cartocdn.com/gl/dark-matter-gl-style/style.json` |
| Voyager | `https://basemaps.cartocdn.com/gl/voyager-gl-style/style.json` |

Appending `-nolabels` to the style name (`positron-nolabels`) drops the place labels,
which is often what you want when the layer carries its own text.

```{julia}
Deck(
    layer,
    initial_view_state = ViewState(longitude = -122.4, latitude = 37.8, zoom = 11),
    map_style = "https://basemaps.cartocdn.com/gl/dark-matter-gl-style/style.json"
)
```

Leaving `map_style` out draws the layers on a blank background, which is what you want for
non-geographic data — see `OrthographicView` on the [Layers page](layers.qmd).

Two things follow from a basemap being a separate map library underneath deck.gl:

- **It always needs network access**, for MapLibre itself and for the map tiles. This is
  true even with `bundle=:local`, which only inlines deck.gl.
- **deck.gl owns the camera.** The basemap follows it, so `initial_view_state` and the
  controller settings apply to both.

## Data Input

DeckGL.jl works with any [Tables.jl](https://tables.juliadata.org/)-compatible data source:

```julia
# NamedTuple of vectors
data = (x = [1, 2, 3], y = [4, 5, 6])

# DataFrame
using DataFrames
df = DataFrame(x = [1, 2, 3], y = [4, 5, 6])

# Vector of NamedTuples
rows = [(x=1, y=4), (x=2, y=5), (x=3, y=6)]
```

### Column References

Use `Symbol` to reference columns for data-driven properties:

```julia
layer = ScatterplotLayer(
    data = data,
    get_position = [:lng, :lat],     # Two columns for position
    get_radius = :size,               # Column for radius
    get_fill_color = [255, 0, 0, 200] # Static color
)
```

### How Data Reaches the Browser

You do not have to think about this, but it explains why some layers behave differently.

Most layers upload their accessors straight to the GPU, so a table is packed
column-by-column into typed arrays and sent as deck.gl's binary form. Nothing is
allocated per row on either side, and for a million points the page is several times
smaller and builds an order of magnitude faster than one row of JSON per record.

Two things follow from that:

- **Columns that cannot be packed** — strings, or variable-length paths — are sent as a
  plain array and read by index instead. `get_text = :name` works exactly as you would
  expect; it just takes a different route.
- **Picking reports an index, not a row object**, because there are no row objects. The
  `tooltip` prop handles this for you by shipping the columns it needs separately:

  ```julia
  ScatterplotLayer(data = df, get_position = [:lng, :lat], tooltip = [:name, :magnitude])
  ```

  Setting `tooltip` turns on `pickable` unless you say otherwise. Pass `true` for every
  column.

Aggregation layers (`HexagonLayer`, `GridLayer`, `HeatmapLayer`, `ContourLayer`,
`ScreenGridLayer`) bin their records before drawing and read each one through its
accessor, so they cannot take binary attributes at all — deck.gl silently produces a
single bin if you give them any. They are sent an index array instead, over the same
packed columns. Picking one selects a bin, so `tooltip = true` shows the bin's own
aggregated values rather than a source row.

## Color Specification

Colors are specified as RGB or RGBA arrays with values 0-255, a hex string, or any
Colors.jl colorant once that package is loaded:

```julia
# RGB (alpha defaults to 255)
color = [255, 0, 0]      # Red

# RGBA (with transparency)
color = [255, 0, 0, 128] # Semi-transparent red

# Hex string
color = "#ff0000"
color = "#ff000080"      # with alpha

# Colors.jl, via a package extension
using Colors
color = colorant"tomato"
```

For data-driven colors, reference a column:

```julia
get_fill_color = :color_column
```

## ViewState

The `ViewState` controls the camera:

```julia
ViewState(
    longitude = -122.4,  # Center longitude
    latitude = 37.8,     # Center latitude
    zoom = 11,           # Zoom level (0-20+)
    pitch = 45,          # Tilt angle (0-60 degrees)
    bearing = 0          # Rotation (0-360 degrees)
)
```

## Display Options

### Open in Browser

```julia
open_html(deck)
```

### Save as HTML File

```julia
save_html(deck, "visualization.html")
```

### Get HTML String

```julia
html_string = to_html(deck)
```

### Jupyter/VS Code

In notebook environments, `Deck` objects display automatically:

```julia
deck  # Displays inline in notebook
```

## Convenience Functions

For quick visualizations, use the convenience functions. These are **not exported** —
names like `scatter`, `lines`, `text`, `hexbin` and `heatmap` would collide with
Plots.jl and Makie.jl — so call them qualified:

```julia
# Scatterplot
DeckGL.scatter(data, :lng, :lat, radius=:size, color=[255, 140, 0])

# Arcs
DeckGL.arcs(data, [:src_lng, :src_lat], [:dst_lng, :dst_lat])

# Hexagonal binning
DeckGL.hexbin(data, :lng, :lat, radius=1000)

# Heatmap
DeckGL.heatmap(data, :lng, :lat, weight=:value)
```

The full set is `scatter`, `arcs`, `lines`, `paths`, `polygons`, `text`, `hexbin`,
`heatmap` and `geojson`. Each returns a `Deck` you can display:

```julia
DeckGL.scatter(data, :lng, :lat) |> open_html
```

If you would rather use them unqualified, import them explicitly:

```julia
using DeckGL
using DeckGL: scatter, heatmap
```

## Multiple Layers

Combine multiple layers in a single visualization:

```julia
layers = [
    ScatterplotLayer(data=points, get_position=[:lng, :lat]),
    TextLayer(data=labels, get_position=[:lng, :lat], get_text=:name),
    PathLayer(data=routes, get_path=:path)
]

deck = Deck(layers, initial_view_state=ViewState(zoom=10))
```
